reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in educational services (NAICS 61) at 39.9% of firms in the latest period, up from 30.0% in the prior period. The survey asks whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and it has been fielded since September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in the material, and it covers the sector as a whole rather than any single segment of it.

The federal government's own posture is set out by the Department of Education, which issued AI guidance for schools covering permissible use, risk, and procurement. The department maintains an inventory of its AI use-cases, and the page describes what those use-cases do: CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation; Grammarly for written communication; Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration; and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. The listed uses also include generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in a variety of programming languages, extracting key points and action items from public documents, generating R code for data analysis, training employees on prompt engineering, automating conversion between related data types such as mapping a county name to its FIPS code, generating mock datasets for testing, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, and testing filters against fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information. The department frames this under Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence, with its OCIO supporting adherence to federal regulations on responsible and secure AI usage.

On the market side, HolonIQ is described as a platform for impact market intelligence covering the global impact economy, and the site's own description of it says it tracks EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning. HolonIQ's page describes capabilities rather than findings: sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, scoring impact with rubrics and ratings, mapping partnership landscapes and alliances, and mapping competitive landscapes. It states that governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms, and investors use it, and that global media rely on it for insight and data on the global impact economy. No dollar figures, funding totals, or adoption rates for education appear in the excerpt.

The material on courses and credentials comes from this site's own catalog rather than from an external authority. It lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, each with one verified source and re-verified daily. The named providers are DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Dataquest, fast.ai, DeepLearning.AI with Stanford on Coursera, Google, Hugging Face, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. Four are university graduate courses with public materials: Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191. The page states that all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, though three, DeepLearning.AI's specializations and Karpathy's and fast.ai's courses, pair that with either a paid certificate option or public code repositories. It notes that university courses are generally structured around exam-driven theory while the industry courses are described as code-first or hands-on, and that only three list an accompanying public code repository. It also states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

What the sources do not provide is as notable as what they do. There is no reported ROI evidence for AI in education, no vendor revenue or funding totals, no breakdown of adoption by K-12 versus higher education versus workforce learning, and no enforcement or compliance actions. The regulatory material is a federal guidance and use-case inventory, not a rule with penalties described here. The Census figure is a single sector-wide adoption share with a prior-period comparison and nothing finer.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few modest conclusions. Adoption in educational services is real and rising, at 39.9% against 30.0% previously, per the Census Bureau. The documented federal uses cluster around drafting and communication assistance, transcription, summarization, code generation, data conversion, and testing of safeguards, which suggests low-stakes administrative and instructional-support tasks are where the concrete examples sit. The Department of Education's guidance frames permissible use, risk, and procurement, so procurement and risk review are part of the federal posture even where the sources do not describe specific requirements. Beyond that, the sources describe market-intelligence capabilities and a course catalog rather than outcomes, so claims about returns, cost savings, or learning gains in this sector are not supported by anything in this material.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
